title: Evaluate paid training-vocabulary codebooks without treating literal escapes as readings
statement: Randomly assigned dictionaries made from 6,253 certain ZL practice-training word types allow repeated non-e glyphs and multi-gallows entries, but coverage and key cost trade off. Across four historical works and three assignment seeds, a 5,000-entry key covers on average 67.0% of tokens and 48–49% of types in the public ZL and IT practice-evaluation samples; its compressed dictionary alone costs 224,376–245,864 bits, or 8.98–9.83 bits per 25,000-token planted test. A reversible escape handles unknown plaintext words, but its output is not constrained to the Voynich glyph inventory. No matching key or real plaintext is inferred from these coverage figures.
check: Build a reviewed cipher family or declarative model with a fully charged dictionary and a historically plausible, bounded escape channel. Calibrate unknown-key recovery, including out-of-vocabulary and boundary tests, on disjoint planted controls at the same budget. Only then register a frozen key or scored family and evaluate held-out manuscript pages against description length and red-team controls. Report dictionary-only, escape-only and combined results separately and include program, dictionary, plaintext and preimage costs.
method: Build an observed ciphertext vocabulary from certain ASCII-lowercase paragraph tokens on public ZL practice-training pages, excluding words beginning with z to reserve that prefix for escapes. For each of Dante, Libro de Buen Amor, the Paston Letters and Jan Hus Postilla, choose the 500, 2,000 or 5,000 most frequent plaintext types in the first 50,000 normalized tokens. Independently shuffle the sorted ciphertext vocabulary with seeds 17, 37 and 73 and assign the first K entries to those plaintext types. Encode the next 25,000 tokens: dictionary words use their assigned ciphertext word; other words use z plus fixed ROT13 on their literal spelling. The z prefix is an escape introducer, not a mandatory terminal glyph. The completed map and escape rule recover every planted test exactly, as asserted. The plaintext frequency training window and test window do not overlap, and the ZL codeword sample is separate from public practice-evaluation ZL and IT pages. Evaluate only dictionary membership of the observed words in the assigned ciphertext side of the key; this is a syntactic coverage measurement, not a prediction that the random paired plaintext is correct. The escape channel can produce non-EVA letters, so its appearance is counted separately from dictionary output.
key_cost: Serialize only {"map": ciphertext-to-plaintext} with vs.judge.canonical and apply vs.judge.compressed_bits (raw LZMA2 preset 9 extreme). Report raw bytes and the compressed bits charged by the judge’s key-cost function, plus compressed key bits divided by 25,000 test tokens. This is a key-only cost: it omits the escape program, plaintext encoding and preimage charges and is not a full judge verdict. The literal escape spends arbitrary unmodeled text and does not make a free dictionary.
boundary_control: The escape syntax accepts arbitrary lowercase words. For unseen a=xxqxqxx and b=qqxqqxq, the two escaped codewords for a and b concatenate to exactly the single escaped codeword for c=a+m+b because ROT13(m)=z. All three are checked absent from the fitted plaintext map. Thus known word spaces remain necessary: removing them yields an ambiguous stream despite the absence of a universal terminator.

results.lexicon_source: ZL public practice-training paragraph words excluding z-prefix

reproduce.instructions: Save the script as /tmp/voy_pl3008_codebook.py; run python3 -m vs fetch, then PYTHONPATH=. python3 /tmp/voy_pl3008_codebook.py. It verifies the input hashes and asserts unique maps and exact plaintext round trips in all 36 settings.

limitations: The ciphertext vocabulary is fitted directly to public Voynich training pages and assignment to plaintext is random; neither the key nor the model is claimed as historical or deciphering. The plaintext dictionary is selected on the preceding portion of the same book, so held-out sections are not independent books. Escape output permits all ASCII letters, including glyphs not recognized as ordinary EVA, and its fixed ROT13 is merely reversible, not a security claim. The presented compressed key bits are not the complete description length or a comparison with the Voynich-only baseline. The existing codebook family does not implement the escape and the trusted scorer does not run this local script. Evaluation uses the public practice split and two readings of the same manuscript, not the secret held-out pages. No claimed language/cipher cell was ruled out.
